articles.title: Therapeutic lactate in critically ill patients: Fuel, fluid, or drug?
articles.summary: Lactate occupies a paradoxical position in critical care. Traditionally regarded as a marker of physiological stress, it is increasingly recognized as an important metabolic substrate with potential therapeutic effects. In their meta-analysis of randomized trials, Labenbacher and colleagues summarize the current clinical evidence for hypertonic sodium lactate treatment (HSL) across heterogeneous critically ill populations. Although no mortality benefit can be established, the available evidence raises several important mechanistic and methodological questions. First, "lactate therapy" is not a single intervention as HSL simultaneously alters lactate availability, sodium load, tonicity, and acid-base balance.

articles.title: Prevalence and Characteristics of Coma in Latin American Critical Care Units: The COMA LATAM Study.
articles.summary: Patients under deep sedation or pharmacological coma induction were excluded unless the coma state preceded pharmacological intervention. Among 8305 critically ill patients, 1145 met coma criteria (point prevalence 13.8%), with country-specific rates ranging from 5.1% to 36.8%. Individual patient data were available for 729 patients (63.7%). Traumatic brain injury was the leading individual cause (24.8%), followed by hypoxic-anoxic brain injury (14.6%) and intracerebral hemorrhage (13.5%). When categorized by pathophysiology, vascular causes predominated (48.6%), followed by traumatic brain injury (24.8%) and other causes (26.6%).

articles.title: From rescue to precision: breaking the salvage-therapy curse in refractory septic shock.
articles.summary: Each has a plausible mechanism, may improve physiological or haemodynamic surrogates, and most remain without definitive evidence of survival benefit in unselected patients. Refractory septic shock is managed with a small core of evidence-based treatments and a growing number of salvage therapies, including methylene blue, the vitamin C cocktail, and several blood purification devices. Recent biomarker-selected evidence with polymyxin B, however, suggests that patient selection may be critical. This article argues that most remain unproven because of how they are deployed and tested, not because their mechanisms fail. Given late to the sickest patients, they are subject to confounding by indication, a ceiling effect on attribution, and responder-biased reporting, which together generate a misleading reputation independent of any true effect.
